Using this instrument, I show that in areas with more use of Pix, deposits of small banks rise relative to large banks. The effects are especially strong for time deposits, where banks compete on interest rates.<sup>1</sup> I also find a significant decline in local deposit market concentration measured as HHI. For instance, if residents of a hypothetical municipality with five banks of equal size increase their value of Pix transactions by R$ 1000 ($200), there will be six banks of equal size within five months in that municipality. As small banks raise more deposits, I show that they also increase their lending, but the effect on lending is limited because large banks have access to alternative sources of financing. 

I assess several competing explanations for the launch-period results. I split municipalities into the ones that reopened before summer 2020 and the ones that reopened during summer 2020. The deposit responses begin around the introduction of Pix among both early and late reopeners, which weighs against the explanation that reopenings are driving the results. Placebo tests show that the effects are unique to November 2020 and do not appear in different timeframes. I also report sensitivity exercises following Altonji et al. (2005) and Rambachan and Roth (2023), to add more evidence to the parallel trends in my setting. 

The reopening evidence does not rule out a national recovery that affects small and large banks differently. I therefore complement it with an instrument based on failures at counterparty banks that disrupt Pix payments, following Ding et al. (2025). These

## _5.3 Assessment of competing explanations_ I assess whether delayed reopening effects, stimulus-related flows, or earlier deposit patterns can explain the bank-group differences and launch-period timing of the findings. I then examine selection into reopening and sensitivity to controls and departures from parallel trends. I use differences in reopening dates to distinguish the Pix response from delayed effects of local recovery. Ministry of Health data identify municipalities that reopened in April or early May 2020 ( _early relaxers_ ) and those that reopened during the summer ( _late relaxers_ ). The September survey confirms that early reopeners had not reinstated restrictions by then. I show in Tables C.33 and C.34 of Appendix C.28 that changes in deposit concentration and deposits of small banks relative to large banks are statistically and economically significant for both groups. Figure 7 shows that the first significant divergence appears around November 2020 among both early and late relaxers, with economically comparable effects. This pattern weighs against an effect occurring at a fixed lag after local reopening. It does not eliminate a recovery paced by national conditions that affects small banks differently from large banks. Stimulus payments could also shift deposits toward large banks, followed by a reversal around the Pix launch. These payments were mainly distributed by Caixa Econˆomica, one of the large banks in my sample. However, in Appendix C.20, I run an event study around COVID stimulus payments to show that there was no significant increase in deposits of small banks in high-Pix areas. In Appendix C.20, I use detailed data on stimulus payments by municipality to show that deposits and deposit shares of large banks do not rise. Deposits of Caixa rise in areas with larger payments, but they reverse within one to three months. I also do not find evidence of spatial correlation between the initial Pix take-up and first-round stimulus payments. Finally, stimulus per capita negatively predicts the relaxation of COVID restrictions, as I show in Appendix C.21, which works against a stimulus-based explanation for stronger Pix take-up in eased municipalities. 32 Figure 7: Impact of Pix on Deposit Market Concentration: IV with Easing of COVID Restrictions, Early and Late Relaxers �

## _5.1 IV: reopening conditions and launch-period results_ 

I exploit an instrumental variable approach to estimate the causal effect of Pix on bank deposits and market power. Specifically, I use municipality-level data on COVID-19 restrictions in Brazil that are constructed by de Souza Santos et al. (2021) in collaboration with the Brazilian Confederation of Municipalities. After the first wave of COVID, during the summer of 2020, many municipalities in Brazil decided to lift COVID restrictions. To understand which municipalities relaxed COVID restrictions, the Brazilian government conducted a survey in September, asking each mayor if the restrictions in their municipality were relaxed. 

The authors surveyed mayors of most Brazilian municipalities and collected information about types of restrictions and their easing. I use the easing of COVID-19 restrictions prior to the introduction of Pix to instrument for Pix usage in the analysis.<sup>12</sup> I denote municipalities that eased COVID restrictions by September 2020 as _treated_ and those that did not as _control_ . I show summary statistics separately for the two groups of municipalities in Appendix C.16. Demographic and economic indicators are fairly similar across the two groups, but there can still be differences in unobservables. For example, the treatment group might have more conservative political views, lower mortality, or younger people.<sup>13</sup> Such differences do not violate the identifying assumptions as long as they do not impact the demand for deposits of small banks in November 2020, when Pix was launched. I also show on a map that there are no visible spatial patterns in areas where the restrictions were relaxed. In addition, in Appendix C.21, I regress the relaxation

The joint response of deposit quantities and rates is consistent with increased demand for small-bank deposits: their deposits rise while their deposit rates fall relative to large banks. A doubling of Pix transaction value is associated with a 14-basis-point narrowing of the deposit-rate gap. Small banks continue to pay higher rates, but improved payment convenience allows them to attract deposits at a smaller premium.<sup>2</sup> 

I test two mechanisms using differences in payment costs before Pix. First, if Pix facilitates moving funds toward higher-yielding accounts, the increase in small-bank time deposits should be stronger where interbank transfers were previously more expensive. I construct expected transfer costs using banks’ transfer fees and local deposit shares, and find a stronger time-deposit response in municipalities with higher pre-Pix costs. Second, if Pix makes small-bank accounts more convenient for everyday payments, checking deposits should respond more where existing retail payment options were costly or less attractive. Consistent with this prediction, the checking-deposit response is stronger in municipalities with higher debit-card fees, lower credit-card rewards, and fewer point-of-sale terminals relative to businesses. 

I also examine whether the results are driven primarily by reallocation from large banks to small banks (intensive margin) or by new accounts opened by previously unbanked households (extensive margin). To do so, I test whether the effects are stronger in areas with a larger share of the banked population. I find that deposits of small banks increase more strongly in more banked areas, while deposits of large banks increase more

## _6.2 Costs of retail payments_ 

The second relevant margin is the cost of retail payments. Before Pix, retail payments in Brazil relied heavily on cash, debit cards, and credit cards. Pix introduced a payment method that is immediate and free for consumers. To the extent that pre-Pix retail payment options were more expensive or less widely accepted, Pix should make transactional accounts at small banks more attractive. Unlike credit or debit cards, Pix does not charge a fee, but it also does not pay any rewards. A related feature of the Brazilian economy is the large informal sector, where card acceptance was historically more limited and cash use more common. There are also switching costs associated with changing payment habits and bank relationships (Illanes (2017)), including the costs of opening and funding accounts at smaller banks. This mechanism should matter primarily for checking deposits, because these balances are used for day-to-day transactions. 

The retail-payment mechanism predicts a stronger checking-deposit response where card payments were more costly or less attractive before Pix. I test this prediction using Central Bank data on debit-card fees and credit-card rewards. I also combine state-level POS-terminal counts with municipality-level data on the number of businesses to split municipalities into those with above- and below-average concentrations of POS terminals as of October 2020. 

Table 10 presents the three comparisons. The estimated increase in checking deposits at small banks relative to large banks is larger in high-debit-fee municipalities (columns 1–2). The response is statistically significant in low-reward municipalities but not in highreward municipalities (columns 3–4).
